opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it's a really interesting tradeoff, and I think people sometimes underestimate how much the tokenizer matters. For Llama 2 we had a 32K vocabulary, and for Llama 3 we went to roughly 128K. The main benefit is compression: with a larger vocabulary, the same text gets encoded into fewer tokens. That means for a fixed amount of compute, the model effectively sees more text during training, and at inference you can fit more actual content into the same context window. It also helps a lot for multilingual data and for code, where a small vocabulary tends to fragment things into lots of tiny pieces.

The cost is mostly on the embedding and output layers. Your input embedding matrix and your softmax over the vocabulary both grow linearly with vocabulary size, so you add parameters and some compute at the last layer. For a very small model that can be a meaningful fraction of the total, but at the scales we're talking about, 8B, 70B and up, it becomes relatively marginal compared to the gains you get from better compression.

There's also a subtler question of whether rare tokens get trained enough. If your vocabulary is huge, some tokens appear very rarely and their embeddings may be undertrained. But when you're training on something like fifteen trillion tokens, that concern shrinks a lot.

So when you put it all together, it was pretty clearly worth it for us. You're trading a small increase in parameters for a model that is more efficient per token, both in training and at inference, and that tends to translate into better performance overall. It's one of those decisions that isn't flashy, but compounds across everything downstream.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the tokenizer was actually one of the first decisions we made for Llama 3, and it's a good example of a change that looks small on paper but touches everything downstream.

So we went from 32k tokens in Llama 2 to 128k. The obvious benefit is compression. With a bigger vocabulary you need fewer tokens to represent the same text, and for us it was roughly 15 percent fewer tokens on English, and much more than that on other languages and on code, where the 32k vocab was really inefficient. Fewer tokens means two things. At training time, for a fixed compute budget, you are effectively seeing more text, so your tokens are more information-dense. And at inference time, generating a response takes fewer forward passes, so it's faster and cheaper for the same output. That's a real win, and it's a win that compounds across the whole lifetime of the model.

Now the costs. The first one is the embedding and output matrices. With 128k vocabulary times the hidden dimension, that's a non-trivial number of parameters, and for a small model like the 8B it's a significant fraction of the total. Those parameters are not doing the same kind of work as the transformer layers. So for the 8B specifically, it's a less obvious tradeoff than for the 70B or the 405B, where the embeddings are a rounding error. We decided to keep one tokenizer across the family because the consistency matters a lot for the ecosystem, for distillation, for people moving between sizes.

The second cost is that each token is seen less often. If you have more tokens, the rare ones get fewer gradient updates, so you need enough training data for those embeddings to actually learn something. At 15 trillion tokens that's fine. If you were training a small model on a few hundred billion tokens, I would be more careful.

And then the third thing, which people underestimate, is that the vocabulary also sets the frontier of what the model can do with reasoning and multilinguality. If a word in Hindi or Thai is split into ten byte-level tokens, the model has to spend capacity just reassembling it before doing anything intelligent. So a larger vocabulary is partly a bet on multilingual quality, and that was a priority for Llama 3.

One subtle point: a bigger vocabulary changes what a "token" means when you compare models. Benchmarks and scaling laws are expressed in tokens, so you have to be careful that your tokens are now worth more. We re-derived our scaling laws with the new tokenizer rather than reusing the Llama 2 numbers.

So overall, my view is that for frontier-scale training, a large vocabulary is almost strictly better, and the main reason not to go even bigger is diminishing returns on compression versus the growing cost of the softmax and the embeddings, especially on the small models. 128k felt like a good point on that curve, and it's also what the rest of the field converged on around the same time, which is a little reassuring.

astra-6.text:
There are two sides to it. With a larger vocabulary, you can represent the same text with fewer tokens. That’s particularly useful for multilingual text and code, and it means you can fit more information into the same context window.

But it’s not free. A larger vocabulary makes the embedding and output layers bigger, so you spend more memory and compute there. And if you keep adding very rare tokens, you get diminishing returns: those tokens take up capacity, but you don’t see them often enough during training to learn them well.

So the goal isn’t to maximize vocabulary size. It’s to find the balance where better compression across the languages and domains you care about is worth the additional cost.

sol-6.1.text:
There’s a tradeoff. With a larger vocabulary, you can represent the same text with fewer tokens. That’s particularly useful for code and multilingual text, where a smaller vocabulary can split things into lots of little pieces. You get more useful content into the same context window, and you need fewer generation steps to produce the same answer.

But the vocabulary isn’t free. You have larger embedding and output matrices, so that adds parameters, memory, and computation. And if you keep adding tokens, some will be very rare, so you don’t necessarily learn good representations for them.

So the objective isn’t to make the vocabulary as large as possible. It’s to find a balance between how efficiently you encode the text and the cost of the model. For Llama 3, increasing it made sense, especially given the importance of code and multilingual capabilities.
